summary: 15 concise trial-paper-only hypotheses distilled from the ResearchAgent run for accord, grouped by per-hypothesis feature attribution.

mechanisms.description: Baseline WMH/ICV in the top quartile (high WMH burden) will lead to greater cognitive decline with intensive systolic BP lowering because extensive white‑matter injury reduces cerebral perfusion reserve and impairs autoregulation, increasing ischemic vulnerability at lower perfusion pressures.

Presence of lacunar infarcts on baseline MRI will increase the risk of stroke and accelerated cognitive decline under intensive BP targets because prior small‑vessel infarction reflects fragile perforating arterioles and diminished autoregulatory capacity that cannot tolerate aggressive reductions in systolic pressure.

Presence of cerebral microbleeds at baseline will modify treatment harm by heightening the likelihood of intracerebral hemorrhage and subsequent cognitive worsening with intensive BP lowering, since microvascular fragility and disrupted vessel integrity predispose to bleeding and secondary ischemia when hemodynamics are altered.

A prespecified high CSVD categorical score (WMH/ICV ≥75th percentile OR ≥1 lacune OR ≥1 microbleed) will magnify cognitive and functional harms from intensive BP lowering because combined markers of small‑vessel disease denote severely impaired cerebrovascular reserve and compromised tissue tolerance to lower systemic pressures.

A medium CSVD burden (WMH/ICV 25–75th percentile with ≤1 lacune and ≤1 microbleed) will attenuate net cognitive benefit of intensive BP control because intermediate small‑vessel pathology limits the brain’s ability to sustain adequate perfusion during lower systolic targets compared with low‑CSVD patients.

Low CSVD at baseline (WMH/ICV <25th percentile with no lacunes or microbleeds) will preserve cognitive trajectories with intensive BP lowering because intact microvasculature and preserved autoregulatory function maintain cerebral perfusion despite reduced systolic pressure, allowing macrovascular benefits to predominate.

Elevated carotid–femoral PWV (≥10 m/s) at baseline will magnify cognitive decline and functional harm from intensive SBP lowering because arterial stiffness impairs dampening of pulsatile flow and reduces cerebral perfusion reserve during lower systemic pressures.

Concomitant elevated PWV (≥10 m/s) and high WMH/ICV will synergistically increase risk of adjudicated falls and orthostatic syncope with intensive BP targets because combined large‑artery stiffness and diffuse white‑matter disease disrupt baroreflex buffering and cerebral autoregulation needed to maintain orthostatic cerebral perfusion.

Elevated PWV in the absence of substantial WMH will still modify treatment effects by increasing hemodynamic instability and thereby attenuating stroke prevention benefits of intensive BP lowering, since central arterial stiffness promotes transmission of pulsatile stress to the cerebral microcirculation despite lower peripheral systolic readings.

Having two or more lacunes at baseline will predispose to greater deterioration in the cognitive slope under intensive BP lowering because multiple prior small‑vessel infarcts exhaust neural network reserve and leave limited tolerance to further reductions in cerebral perfusion.

A single microbleed on baseline MRI will predict disproportionate all‑cause mortality with intensive BP lowering due to increased susceptibility to hemorrhagic complications and secondary ischemic injury in a diffusely fragile microvascular bed when systemic pressures are aggressively lowered.

Increasing continuous WMH/ICV burden (modeled as a graded baseline characteristic) will show a dose‑dependent decrease in cognitive resilience to intensive BP lowering because progressive white‑matter pathology incrementally narrows perfusion reserve and raises susceptibility to ischemia at lower systolic targets.

Discordance characterized by low WMH/ICV but elevated PWV at baseline will modify outcomes by preserving some cognitive resilience while still exposing patients to cardiovascular and hemodynamic risks under intensive BP lowering, since large‑artery stiffness impairs central hemodynamic buffering even when parenchymal injury is limited.

Baseline coexistence of microbleeds and lacunes will amplify incident stroke risk with intensive BP lowering because combined hemorrhagic and ischemic small‑vessel pathology signifies diffuse vascular fragility that cannot tolerate aggressive reductions in systolic pressure without precipitating new vascular events.

Concurrent high CSVD (WMH/ICV ≥75th percentile or ≥1 lacune or microbleed) together with elevated PWV (≥10 m/s) at baseline will blunt the reduction in major adverse cardiovascular events with intensive BP lowering because the combination of microvascular dysfunction and central arterial stiffness sustains end‑organ hemodynamic stress despite lower peripheral systolic targets.
